extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, congressional staff, defense policymakers, and agency officials evaluating A-76 competitive sourcing policy
extracted.subtask_description: Policy-oriented guidance and legislative options for how Congress (and agencies) should oversee, modify, or limit competitive sourcing (OMB Circular A-76) — with special focus on military medical facilities and the Walter Reed case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require specific reporting on the status of ongoing A-76 competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may direct DOD to provide more detailed information on the status of ongoing A-76 studies, including quarterly updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports could include: the number of older competitions under review and whether they have waivers; status of new standard multi-function A-76 studies, including how many exceed the 12-month limitation and how many have waivers; number of competitions in excess of 18 months (with/without waivers); number in excess of 30 months (with/without waivers); and demographics of affected government employees and whether any particular group is adversely impacted by the A-76 policy, process, or outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit establishment of numerical quotas for A-76 studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could prohibit the establishment of numerical quotas for federal agencies to conduct A-76 studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Desire to meet numerical quotas (or targets) may drive agencies to continue problematic competitions; prohibition would remove this incentive. (See reference to proposed Section 323 of H.R. 4986.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare activities at military medical facilities inherently governmental
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could declare that any activities on military medical facilities that affect patient care be considered inherently governmental and not appropriate for competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One legislative approach is to declare all activities at military medical facilities as inherently governmental and not subject to competition; rationale is that activities touching the military patient may be critical to mission success and should be performed by federal employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose a moratorium or prohibit competitions at military medical facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could impose a one-year moratorium or otherwise prohibit the conduct of future A-76 competitions at military medical facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Representative Ortiz's amendment (House-passed H.R. 1538) proposing a one-year moratorium on A-76 competitions at DOD medical facilities to review whether A-76 sacrifices service or performance of the mission. The amendment would address only future competitions and calls for a report assessing A-76's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit inclusion of health care and retirement costs in A-76 cost comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could prohibit including health care and retirement costs in the A-76 cost comparison process where DOD contributes more (per employee for health care) than the contractor, and could exclude retirement costs to avoid rewarding lower contractor benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reportedly the Army failed to exclude health care costs as required by the Defense Appropriations bill; excluding these costs would prevent contractors from being advantaged by offering lower benefits than the federal government. (See proposed Section 322 under H.R. 4986.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply minimum cost differential and adjust contractor bids for disruption/productivity losses
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost comparisons should account for the 'minimum cost differential' required by federal rules to reflect costs associated with disruption and loss of productivity related to the competition process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An AFGE observer stated the Army's analysis failed to account for a $10 million minimum cost differential; failing to apply required differentials can render government cost estimates 'demonstrably flawed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a rotating team of experienced acquisition professionals to serve as Agency Tender Officials (ATOs)
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB could establish a team of experienced A-76 professionals who could be called upon to serve as ATOs in competitions outside their assigned agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATOs should be selected to serve across agencies, require sufficient funds to represent federal employees throughout the competition (including post-award), and have a certain independence. This addresses the problem of fragmented/unclear authority in complex competitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require enforcement of A-76 rules and provide authority to stop noncompliant competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could ensure that A-76 rules are followed and create authority or mechanisms to enforce the rules, including stopping competitions that exceed permitted lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When A-76 rules are not followed there is no authority to ensure integrity; examples include OMB or DOD potentially stopping competitions that exceed time limits and enforcing statutory exclusions (e.g., health care cost exclusions). Effective enforcement could change outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant federal employees rights equivalent to private-sector contractors (protest rights and support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could grant federal employees the right to directly protest competition outcomes (or otherwise ensure parity), and require agencies to fund representation for federal employees during all phases of competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically contractors could protest at GAO while federal employees could not; P.L. 108-375 expanded 'interested party' to include ATOs, but employees still lacked direct protest rights. Options include granting direct protest rights to employees, ensuring ATOs can file, and prohibiting agencies from conducting competitions unless they can fund employee representation through post-award processes (see proposed Section 326 of H.R. 4986).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require agencies have sufficient funding to conduct competitions, including employee representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could prohibit federal agencies from conducting competitions unless they have enough funds to fully fund competitions, including representation for federal employees throughout all phases, up to post-award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses the problem where agency managers lack legal expertise or resources to advocate for employees; guaranteeing funding would enable proper appeals and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage alternatives to A-76 such as High-Performing Organizations (HPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could provide incentives and encouragement for agencies to explore alternatives to A-76, including development of high-performing organizations to achieve efficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO's Commercial Activities Panel recommended HPOs; given federal employees winning many competitions, agencies might pursue alternatives that avoid costs and challenges associated with A-76.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancel outstanding A-76 studies conducted under the pre-2003 Circular
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could direct cancellation of any outstanding competitions conducted under the pre-2003 A-76 Circular to avoid recurring problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AFGE recommended cancellation of long-running studies (example: Keesler AFB competition reportedly at least eight years in process). Cancelling pre-2003 studies could prevent further flawed outcomes tied to the old Circular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit A-76 applicability during declared war or military mobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The A-76 circular allows the Department of Defense Competitive Sourcing Official to determine whether the circular applies during declared war or mobilization; Congress/DoD can opt out during such times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During declared war or mobilization, DoD may choose to opt-out of A-76 to avoid destabilizing critical operations and staffing; Walter Reed's experience suggests competitions during such times can have destabilizing effects on civilian workforce and patient care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accelerate BRAC implementation and fund maintenance to prevent operational decline
rubrics_metrics.description: Secretary of Defense should seek legislative approval to accelerate Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) implementation and release funds to start construction of the new Walter Reed National Military Medical Center to avoid existing facilities 'dying on the vine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposal: accelerate or waive the Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) and release monies required for construction; fund existing facilities to maintain full operation until closure so servicemembers and families do not experience service delays.
